summary: Suggests a pair of TCP options for using alternate data checksum algorithms in the TCP header. The use is experimental and not recommended in production. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1146 and RFC 6247.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1145 proposes experimental TCP options for choosing a checksum algorithm and carrying extra checksum data when needed. The RFC says these options are not recommended for production use; RFC 1146 and RFC 6247 later replaced it.

questions: how does tcp negotiate an alternate checksum
subtitle: Experimental TCP options for negotiating an alternate data checksum

tldr.problem: Some users wanted TCP checksums with different error-detection properties or longer checksum values.
tldr.mechanism: Two TCP options request a checksum algorithm during connection setup and carry extra checksum data when the result exceeds 16 bits.
tldr.outcome: The RFC says the options are experimental and not recommended for production; it was later replaced by RFC 1146 and RFC 6247.

today: RFC 1145 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 1146 and RFC 6247.

sections.title: Why Use an Alternate Checksum
sections.content:
The RFC responds to interest in checksums with error-detection and correction properties different from the standard TCP checksum. It proposes negotiating an alternate algorithm when a connection is established and carrying extra information for algorithms with checksums longer than 16 bits.

The memo explicitly describes use of these options as experimental and not recommended for production use.
sections.plainLanguage: Some users wanted TCP checks that behave differently from the standard one. This proposal lets both ends agree on an alternate check when they start a connection.

sections.title: The Request and Data Options
sections.content:
The Alternate Checksum Request option has kind 14 and length 3. Its checksum field identifies the algorithm: 0 is the TCP checksum, 1 is the 8-bit Fletcher algorithm, and 2 is the 16-bit Fletcher algorithm. The 8-bit algorithm produces a 16-bit checksum; the 16-bit algorithm produces a 32-bit checksum.

The Alternate Checksum Data option has kind 15 and carries checksum data when the chosen value is longer than 16 bits. That data may be split between the TCP header checksum field and the option, or placed entirely in the option with the header field set to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The request option names the checksum method. If its result is too large for the TCP checksum field, the data option carries the extra checksum bytes.

sections.title: Negotiation and Fallback
sections.content:
A TCP may include the request option in a SYN segment. If both the SYN and SYN-ACK include it and name the same algorithm, the connection uses that algorithm after the handshake. Otherwise, the connection uses the standard TCP checksum.

SYN and RST segments always use the standard checksum. An implementation that does not support the option silently ignores it, which causes the peers to use the standard checksum. An invalid checksum data length requires discarding the segment, sending an RST segment and aborting the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must request the same algorithm. If they do not, or one side ignores the option, they use the standard checksum instead.
